title: Scientists See Tiny Particles Make Ripples in a Super-Hot 'Soup'
summary:
Right after the universe began, it was trillions of degrees hot. Tiny bits called quarks and gluons zoomed around in a hot "soup" called quark-gluon plasma. It lasted only a few millionths of a second.

Today, scientists can make tiny drops of this soup at CERN's Large Hadron Collider in Switzerland. They smash heavy atoms, like lead, together very fast.

Now a team led by physicists from MIT has found that quarks leave wakes as they move through the plasma. It is like a duck making ripples on a pond. This shows the plasma acts like a liquid, with waves, splashes and swirls.

"Now we see the plasma is incredibly dense," said MIT physicist Yen-Jie Lee. He said it can even slow down a quark.

The team used a new way to spot the wakes. Measuring them may help scientists learn about the universe's first moments.
why_it_matters: It helps us understand how the stuff that makes up you and everything around you first formed.

background_read: Everything around us is made of atoms, and atoms are made of even smaller bits like quarks.
When the universe was brand new, it was so hot that these tiny bits could not stick together.
Scientists use giant machines to smash atoms together so they can study what the early universe was like.
